title: Holography: From Black Holes to Quantum Codes and Deep Learning
subtitle: An intuitive, visual course on the AdS/CFT correspondence: the maths you need, the string theory origin, entanglement as geometry, and the bridges to quantum error correction and deep learning
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: Holography says that a world with gravity can be described by a quantum theory on its boundary. This course builds the idea from the ground up in 13 chapters: black hole entropy, the geometry of hyperbolic and anti-de Sitter space, entanglement and conformal field theory, strings, D-branes and Maldacena's duality, the holographic dictionary, the Ryu-Takayanagi formula, black holes and wormholes, tensor networks, quantum error correction, the bridge to deep learning, the Page curve and islands, and a final chapter that ties it all together. The maths is introduced with pictures and worked formulas: 35 numbered figures (hyperbolic tilings and geodesics are computed, not sketched), numbered tables, a recap, a memory trick, an expanded ELI5 and a concept map in every chapter. 13 interactive labs with 40 levels: walk the hyperbolic disk, measure entanglement with minimal curves, heat AdS until a black hole forms, cut tensor networks, run an exact three-qutrit code, train a network's geometry from entanglement data by gradient descent, evaporate a 12-qubit black hole, and in the capstone build a toy holographic universe that is at once a geometry, a code, a trained network and a black hole. Sources and credits: chapter 10 follows the outline of the Quantum Error Correction lesson of the open AdS/CFT course at adscft.org; chapter 11 presents Yi-Zhuang You's Perimeter Institute talk 'Tensor Network Holography and Deep Learning' (PIRSA:17110111) and the work of Hashimoto and collaborators. The text, figures and labs are original and written for beginners; the labs are toy models that illustrate the mechanisms, not full AdS/CFT.

chapters.title: The holographic idea

maps.title: Holography
links: Holography | starts from | Black hole entropy

summary: Black holes have entropy, and that entropy is proportional to the area of the horizon, not to the volume inside. This one fact suggests that the information in a region of space with gravity can be stored on its surface.
The holographic principle says exactly that: a world with gravity can be fully described by a theory without gravity living on its boundary, with one dimension fewer.
This course builds the idea step by step: the geometry, the string theory example that made it precise, the link to entanglement, and the modern bridges to quantum error correction and deep learning.

glossary.def: A count of how many microscopic arrangements look the same from outside; roughly, hidden information.
The surface around a black hole from which nothing can return.
The entropy of a black hole: one quarter of its horizon area in Planck units.
About 1.6 x 10^-35 metres: the scale where gravity and quantum mechanics meet.
The idea that everything inside a region with gravity can be described by data on its boundary.
The bulk is the inside, with gravity. The boundary is the edge, where the equivalent theory without gravity lives.
Two descriptions that look different but describe the same physics.

keyPoints: Black hole entropy is S = A/4G: proportional to area, not volume.
No region can hold more entropy than a black hole that fills it.
So the true number of degrees of freedom of gravity scales like a surface.
Holography: bulk gravity in d+1 dimensions = boundary quantum theory in d dimensions.
AdS/CFT (1997) is the first exact example, found in string theory.

items: ELI5. Imagine a toy box. You would think the number of toys it can hold depends on how big the inside is. Now imagine a magic box where the number of toys depends only on how much wrapping paper covers the outside. That is strange, and it is how black holes behave.

Now the real words. A black hole's entropy, its amount of hidden information, is a quarter of the area of its horizon measured in tiny Planck squares: S = A/4G. No region can hold more than a black hole that fills it.

So the information in a world with gravity fits on its surface. The holographic principle says the inside (the bulk) and a theory on the surface (the boundary) are two descriptions of the same thing. AdS/CFT is the first exact example.
Try it. In the lab, double the black hole's radius and watch the entropy go up four times, not eight.
If you remember one thing: with gravity, information counts by area, so the surface can describe the inside.

Start with a puzzle. Take a box of gas. Its entropy, the amount of hidden information in the jiggling of its molecules, grows with the volume of the box. Double every side and the entropy goes up eight times. Everything in ordinary physics works like this.

Black holes do not. In the early 1970s Jacob Bekenstein argued that a black hole must have entropy, or else you could destroy entropy by throwing things in. Stephen Hawking then showed that black holes glow with a temperature, which fixed the formula exactly. (See Figure 1.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.1. A black hole's entropy counts the area of its horizon in Planck-sized patches.

items: Here $A$ is the area of the horizon and $\ell_P \approx 1.6\times10^{-35}$ m is the Planck length. In words: one unit of entropy for every four tiny Planck squares on the horizon. The formula contains $G$ (gravity), $\hbar$ (quantum mechanics), $c$ (relativity) and $k_B$ (heat).
It is the one equation we have that needs all four. (See Table 1.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 1.1. How entropy grows when the radius doubles
head: System
Entropy follows

Typical size
rows: about 10^24 for a litre of air
about 10^66 bits for a marble-sized region

items: Now the strange consequence. Try to pack more and more entropy into a region. Eventually there is so much energy that it collapses into a black hole, and a black hole's entropy is its area over four.

So a black hole is the most entropy you can ever fit, and the limit is set by the surface. The volume inside is, in a sense, an illusion: there are not enough independent degrees of freedom to fill it.

Gerard 't Hooft (1993) and Leonard Susskind (1994) took this seriously and proposed the holographic principle: a region of space with gravity can be completely described by a theory living on its boundary. The name comes from holograms, where a flat film stores a full three-dimensional image.
(See Figure 1.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.2. The bulk, with gravity, and the boundary theory, without gravity, are two descriptions of the same physics.

items: For a few years this was a bold guess. Then in 1997 Juan Maldacena found a precise example inside string theory, now called AdS/CFT. On one side: gravity (in fact string theory) in a curved space called anti-de Sitter space, AdS.
On the other: an ordinary quantum field theory with no gravity at all, a conformal field theory or CFT, living on the boundary of that space. (See Table 1.2 below.)

lesson.title: Table 1.2. The two sides of a holographic duality
head: Bulk
Boundary
rows: the boundary theory is strongly coupled
the boundary theory is weakly coupled

items: Why should you care? Because it turns the hardest question in physics, what is quantum gravity, into a question about an ordinary quantum system.

And because working out how the bulk is hidden in the boundary has uncovered surprising links: space is stitched from entanglement, the stitching is a quantum error-correcting code, and the layered structure looks a lot like a deep neural network.

The road ahead: chapters 2 to 4 give you the maths with pictures (curved space, AdS, entanglement and CFTs). Chapters 5 and 6 give the string theory origin and the dictionary. Chapters 7 to 9 link entanglement to geometry.
Chapters 10 to 12 are the bridges to error correction, deep learning and black hole information. Chapter 13 puts everything in one lab.
Memory trick: A quarter of the area. Black hole entropy is a Quarter of the Area: S = A/4. Surface, not stuffing.

summary: Geometry starts with a rule for measuring distance, called the metric. Change the rule and you change the shape of space.
Hyperbolic space is the negatively curved cousin of the sphere: a saddle at every point. It has exponentially more room than flat space, and its boundary is infinitely far away.
You will learn to read a metric, to recognise curvature from triangles and circles, and to draw hyperbolic space as a disk and as a half-plane with a depth coordinate z.

glossary.def: The rule that turns small coordinate steps into real distance.
The shortest path between two points: the 'straight line' of a curved space.
How much a space bends: positive like a sphere, zero like a plane, negative like a saddle.
The two-dimensional space of constant negative curvature.
A map of the whole hyperbolic plane inside a disk; the rim is infinitely far away.
Another map of the same space, with a depth coordinate z and the boundary at z = 0.
A map that keeps angles right but changes sizes.

keyPoints: A metric ds² tells you the real length of a small step.
Curvature shows in triangles: angle sums above 180° (sphere), equal (flat), below (hyperbolic).
Poincaré disk: ds² = 4(dx² + dy²)/(1 − r²)²; distance to the centre is 2 artanh r.
A hyperbolic circle of radius ρ has circumference 2π sinh ρ: exponential room.
Half-plane: ds² = (dx² + dz²)/z²; moving deeper (larger z) is zooming out.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, The holographic idea:
• Black hole entropy is S = A/4G: proportional to area, not volume.
• No region can hold more entropy than a black hole that fills it.
• So the true number of degrees of freedom of gravity scales like a surface.
• Holography: bulk gravity in d+1 dimensions = boundary quantum theory in d dimensions.
• AdS/CFT (1997) is the first exact example, found in string theory.

ELI5. Imagine a map of a magical land drawn on a round plate. Near the edge of the plate everything is drawn smaller and smaller, so a traveller walking towards the edge never gets there. The land is infinite, but the whole map fits on the plate.

Now the real words. The rule for measuring real distance is called the metric. Hyperbolic space has negative curvature: triangles have angles adding to less than 180 degrees and circles have far more room around them than in flat space.
The Poincaré disk is its map on a plate. A second map, the half-plane, has a depth coordinate z, with real lengths divided by z. Stretching the map and going deeper are the same thing: depth is zoom.
Try it. In the lab, drag a point towards the rim and watch the real distance grow without limit while the dot barely moves.
If you remember one thing: the metric makes the shape, and in hyperbolic space going deeper means zooming out.
How far apart are two points? On flat paper, Pythagoras answers: a small step $dx$ across and $dy$ up has length given by

This formula is called the metric. It is the single most important object in geometry, because everything else, lengths of curves, angles, areas, straight lines, follows from it. A different metric means a different space.

On a sphere of radius $R$, with latitude-like angle $\theta$ and longitude $\phi$, the metric is $ds^2 = R^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2)$. The $\sin^2\theta$ says that a step in longitude is shorter near the poles. That one factor is what makes a sphere curved.
You can detect curvature without leaving the surface. Draw a triangle with the straightest possible sides and add up its angles. (See Figure 2.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.1. Triangles reveal curvature: more than 180° on a sphere, less than 180° on a saddle.

items: Hyperbolic space is the opposite of a sphere: negative curvature, the same at every point. It cannot be built in ordinary 3D space without crumpling, so we draw maps of it instead, just as we draw flat maps of the round Earth. The most famous map is the Poincaré disk. (See Figure 2.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.2. The Poincaré disk tiled with identical pentagons. Gold and green curves are straight lines of this space.

items: Read the formula slowly. The top is ordinary flat distance on the map. The bottom, $(1-r^2)^2$, shrinks to zero at the rim $r = 1$, so real distances blow up there. A step that looks tiny near the rim is as long as a big step in the middle. Every pentagon in the figure is the same real size.
Three facts follow. First, the real distance from the centre to a point at map radius $r$ is
which goes to infinity as $r \to 1$: the rim is infinitely far away. Second, straight lines (geodesics) are arcs of circles that hit the rim at right angles, or diameters.
Third, there is a huge amount of room: a circle of real radius $\rho$ has circumference $2\pi\sinh\rho$, which grows exponentially, instead of the flat $2\pi\rho$. (See Table 2.1 below.)

There is a second map of the same space that physicists use even more, because it has a coordinate that will become the star of this course. Cut the disk open and flatten the rim into a straight line. You get the upper half-plane, with $x$ along the boundary and $z > 0$ measuring depth.
(See Figure 2.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.3. The half-plane model. All boxes are the same real size; deeper boxes look bigger on the map.

items: $L$ is the curvature radius: it sets the overall size. The key feature is a symmetry. Multiply both $x$ and $z$ by the same number, $x \to \lambda x$, $z \to \lambda z$, and $ds^2$ does not change. So zooming the boundary by $\lambda$ is the same as moving deeper by a factor $\lambda$.
Depth is scale. Keep that sentence; it is half of holography. (See Table 2.2 below.)

rows: the map itself is drawn flat
real lengths are map lengths divided by z
the boundary: infinitely far away, everything looks huge
deep in the bulk: a long way on the map is a short real distance
a symmetry: zooming equals moving in depth

items: Memory trick: Rim is far, depth is scale. In hyperbolic maps the Rim is infinitely faR, and going Deeper is Zooming out: z is the zoom.

summary: Anti-de Sitter space, AdS, is hyperbolic space with time added: a universe with constant negative curvature. It is the stage on which holography is best understood.
AdS behaves like a box. Its boundary is infinitely far away in distance, yet light gets there and back in a finite time, and anything you throw falls back to the middle.
The symmetries of AdS are exactly the symmetries of a scale-invariant theory living on its boundary. That match is the first hint of the duality.

glossary.def: Space and time together, with a metric that measures both.
The spacetime of constant negative curvature; a solution of Einstein's equations with negative cosmological constant.
The curvature length scale of AdS.
The part of AdS covered by coordinates (t, x, z) with boundary at z = 0.
The whole of AdS, drawn as a solid cylinder.
The edge of AdS at infinity, where the dual theory lives.
A symmetry of a space: a motion that keeps all distances the same.

keyPoints: Poincaré AdS: ds² = (L²/z²)(−dt² + dx² + dz²), boundary at z = 0.
Global AdS is a solid cylinder; its wall is the boundary, time runs up.
AdS is a box: light reaches the boundary and returns in finite time; thrown objects fall back.
Scaling (t, x, z) → λ(t, x, z) is a symmetry: boundary zoom = bulk depth.
The symmetry group of AdS in d+1 dimensions equals the conformal group in d dimensions.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Maths toolkit 1: distance and curved space:
• A metric ds² tells you the real length of a small step.
• Curvature shows in triangles: angle sums above 180° (sphere), equal (flat), below (hyperbolic).
• Poincaré disk: ds² = 4(dx² + dy²)/(1 − r²)²; distance to the centre is 2 artanh r.
• A hyperbolic circle of radius ρ has circumference 2π sinh ρ: exponential room.
• Half-plane: ds² = (dx² + dz²)/z²; moving deeper (larger z) is zooming out.

ELI5. Imagine a huge bowl with sides that get steeper and steeper. Roll a marble from the middle as hard as you like: it always rolls back, and oddly it always takes the same time. Shine a torch and the light reaches the far-off rim and bounces back.

Now the real words. Anti-de Sitter space, AdS, is hyperbolic space with time added. Its metric is ds² = (L²/z²)(−dt² + dx² + dz²) and its boundary is at z = 0, infinitely far away, yet light gets there and back in a finite time.
Everything is pulled towards the middle, so AdS is like a box. Its symmetries are exactly those of a theory on the boundary that looks the same at every zoom, a conformal field theory.
Try it. In the lab, throw the ball gently, then hard, and see that it returns at the same moment.
If you remember one thing: AdS is a box with a far-away wall, and its symmetries match a scale-free theory on that wall.

To get a universe, add time. In relativity the metric measures intervals in spacetime, and time enters with a minus sign: flat spacetime has $ds^2 = -dt^2 + dx^2$ (with the speed of light set to 1). Light travels along paths with $ds^2 = 0$.
Anti-de Sitter space is the spacetime version of the hyperbolic plane. Take the half-plane metric from the last chapter and put a flat spacetime where the single $x$ used to be:

This is AdS in Poincaré coordinates. If $\vec x$ has $d-1$ components, the bulk has $d+1$ dimensions in total and the boundary at $z=0$ has $d$. You can picture it as a stack of flat spacetimes, one for each depth $z$, each magnified by the factor $L/z$. (See Figure 3.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 3.1. The Poincaré patch as a stack of flat worlds. Depth z plays the role of scale.

items: AdS solves Einstein's equations when empty space has a negative energy density, a negative cosmological constant. Our own universe has a small positive one, so we do not live in AdS. It is studied because it is the cleanest laboratory for quantum gravity we have.

The Poincaré coordinates cover only part of the space. The whole thing, global AdS, is best drawn as a solid cylinder: each horizontal slice is a hyperbolic disk, time runs upwards, and the wall of the cylinder is the boundary. (See Figure 3.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 3.2. Global AdS as a cylinder. A thrown ball oscillates; light bounces off the boundary.

items: Here $\rho$ is the real distance from the central axis and $d\Omega^2$ is the metric on a sphere of directions. The factor $\cosh^2\rho$ in front of $dt^2$ is a gravitational potential that rises without limit as you move out.
Climbing costs more and more energy, so everything rolls back to the middle.
Two consequences make AdS feel like a box. A ball thrown from the centre always returns, and it returns after the same time, $\pi L$, however hard you throw it: AdS is a perfect spring.

And a flash of light reaches the boundary in time $\pi L/2$ and comes back, even though the boundary is infinitely far away in distance. Clocks near the boundary run fast compared with the centre by the factor $\cosh\rho$, which makes this possible. (See Table 3.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 3.1. AdS at a glance
head: Property
Statement
Why it matters
rows: reaches the boundary and returns in time πL
clocks differ by cosh ρ (or L/z)
high energy at the boundary = low energy seen deep inside

items: Now the hint of the duality. Look at the symmetries, the motions that leave the metric unchanged. In Poincaré AdS you can shift $t$ and $\vec x$, rotate and boost them, and, as in the last chapter, rescale everything together: $(t,\vec x,z)\to\lambda(t,\vec x,z)$.
Together with a few less obvious ones they form a group called $SO(d,2)$.

Now forget the bulk and think of a quantum field theory in $d$ dimensions that looks the same at all scales. Its symmetries are shifts, rotations, boosts, rescalings and so-called special conformal transformations.

That group is also $SO(d,2)$. The symmetries of AdS are exactly the symmetries of a conformal field theory on its boundary. Symmetry alone does not prove the duality, but it tells you where to look. (See Table 3.2 below.)

summary: The boundary theory is a quantum system, so you need two quantum ideas: entanglement, and the entropy that measures it.
The boundary theory is also a conformal field theory, a quantum theory that looks the same at every scale. Its operators have scaling dimensions, and its correlations fall off as power laws.

How entanglement entropy grows with the size of a region tells you what kind of state you have. For a critical one-dimensional system it grows like a logarithm, with a coefficient called the central charge.

glossary.def: A quantum two-level system: a combination of |0> and |1>.
A link between parts of a quantum system such that only the whole has a definite state.
The description of a part of a quantum system when the rest is ignored.
S = −Tr ρ log ρ: how mixed (random) a density matrix is.
I(A:B) = S(A) + S(B) − S(AB): how much two parts share.
A quantum field theory with scale (and conformal) symmetry.
The number that says how an operator changes when you zoom.
A number that counts the degrees of freedom of a two-dimensional CFT.

keyPoints: An entangled pair is pure as a whole, but each half alone is mixed.
Entanglement entropy S(A) = −Tr ρ_A log ρ_A; for a pure whole, S(A) = S(rest).
Mutual information I(A:B) = S(A) + S(B) − S(AB) is never negative.
CFT correlations are power laws: ⟨O(x)O(0)⟩ = 1/|x|^(2Δ).
Entropy growth: constant (gapped), (c/3) ln ℓ (critical), proportional to ℓ (thermal).

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Anti-de Sitter space:
• Poincaré AdS: ds² = (L²/z²)(−dt² + dx² + dz²), boundary at z = 0.
• Global AdS is a solid cylinder; its wall is the boundary, time runs up.
• AdS is a box: light reaches the boundary and returns in finite time; thrown objects fall back.
• Scaling (t, x, z) → λ(t, x, z) is a symmetry: boundary zoom = bulk depth.
• The symmetry group of AdS in d+1 dimensions equals the conformal group in d dimensions.

ELI5. Imagine two magic coins. Each one alone lands heads or tails at random. But they always land the same way as each other, however far apart they are. The pair has a secret that neither coin has alone. And imagine a pattern, like a snowflake curve, that looks the same however much you zoom in.

Now the real words. The coins are entangled qubits. The randomness of one part of an entangled system is measured by entanglement entropy, S = −Tr ρ log ρ. If the whole is in one definite state, a part and the rest have equal entropy.

A conformal field theory is a quantum theory that looks the same at every scale; its correlations fall off as power laws set by scaling dimensions. In a critical one-dimensional system the entropy of a block grows like (c/3) ln ℓ.
Try it. In the lab, turn the dial to 45 degrees and measure 20 pairs: each side looks random, but they always agree.
If you remember one thing: entanglement means the whole is certain while the parts are random, and its amount is an entropy.

A qubit is the smallest quantum system. It can be in state $|0\rangle$, state $|1\rangle$, or a combination $a|0\rangle + b|1\rangle$ with $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$. Measure it and you get 0 with probability $|a|^2$.
Two qubits can be in a product state like $|0\rangle|0\rangle$, where each has its own state. Or they can be entangled, as in the Bell state:

In a Bell state neither qubit has a state of its own. Measure the first and you get 0 or 1 at random, but the second always agrees. The pair is perfectly definite; each half is perfectly random. (See Figure 4.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.1. A product state and an entangled state. Entropy of a part measures entanglement with the rest.

items: To describe one half alone we use a density matrix $\rho_A$, obtained by averaging over everything about the other half (the partial trace). For the Bell state, $\rho_A$ says: 0 or 1 with probability one half each. The von Neumann entropy measures that randomness:
where $p_i$ are the probabilities in $\rho_A$. For the Bell state $S(A) = \log 2$, one bit. For a product state $S(A)=0$.

When the whole system is in a single definite (pure) state, this entropy is entirely due to entanglement, and it is the same for a region and for everything else: $S(A) = S(\bar A)$. (See Table 4.1 below.)

items: Now the second ingredient. A quantum field theory has degrees of freedom at every point of space. A conformal field theory, CFT, is one with no built-in length scale: zoom in or out and it looks the same.
Systems at a critical point, such as water at its critical temperature or a magnet at the Curie point, are described by CFTs. (See Figure 4.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.2. Scale invariance, and the power-law correlations it forces.

items: In a CFT every operator $O$ (a thing you can measure at a point) has a scaling dimension $\Delta$. Zoom by a factor $\lambda$ and $O$ is multiplied by $\lambda^{-\Delta}$. Symmetry then fixes how two measurements a distance $x$ apart are correlated:

A power law, with no special distance at which correlations die. Compare a gapped system, where correlations fall like $e^{-x/\xi}$ beyond a correlation length $\xi$. The list of operators and their dimensions is most of what defines a CFT.
Put the two ingredients together and ask: how entangled is a region of length $\ell$ with the rest? The answer depends dramatically on the state. (See Figure 4.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.3. Area law, logarithmic law and volume law for entanglement entropy in one dimension.

items: This is the result for the ground state of a CFT in one space dimension. $\epsilon$ is a tiny cutoff length (the lattice spacing) and $c$ is the central charge, which counts how many degrees of freedom the theory has.
A free boson has $c=1$. Holographic CFTs have enormous $c$. Remember this formula: in chapter 7 it will reappear as the length of a curve in hyperbolic space. (See Table 4.2 below.)

summary: String theory replaces point particles with tiny vibrating strings. Closed loops of string give gravity; open strings, whose ends sit on surfaces called D-branes, give the kind of forces found in particle physics.

A stack of N D-branes can be described in two ways: as a gauge theory living on the branes, or as a curved spacetime that the branes create. Maldacena realised that at low energies these two descriptions must be the same theory.
The result is the AdS/CFT correspondence, with a precise map between the knobs of the gauge theory (N and the coupling) and the size and quantum-ness of the curved space.

glossary.def: A tiny one-dimensional object whose vibrations appear as different particles.
The typical size of a string.
A surface on which open strings can end; a D3-brane has three space dimensions.
A quantum theory of force-carrying fields, like the theory of gluons.
The number of branes, and the number of 'colours' of the gauge theory.
λ = g²N: the effective strength of the gauge theory at large N.
The highly symmetric gauge theory that lives on D3-branes; it is a CFT.
Five-dimensional AdS times a five-dimensional sphere: the space near the branes.

keyPoints: Closed strings contain gravity; open strings on D-branes give gauge theory.
N D3-branes: gauge theory SU(N) on the branes, or a curved throat AdS5 × S5.
Maldacena: N = 4 super Yang-Mills = string theory on AdS5 × S5.
L/ℓs = λ^(1/4): strong coupling means a big, gently curved space.
G ∝ 1/N²: many colours means classical gravity.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Maths toolkit 2: entanglement and conformal field theory:
• An entangled pair is pure as a whole, but each half alone is mixed.
• Entanglement entropy S(A) = −Tr ρ_A log ρ_A; for a pure whole, S(A) = S(rest).
• Mutual information I(A:B) = S(A) + S(B) − S(AB) is never negative.
• CFT correlations are power laws: ⟨O(x)O(0)⟩ = 1/|x|^(2Δ).
• Entropy growth: constant (gapped), (c/3) ln ℓ (critical), proportional to ℓ (thermal).

ELI5. Imagine tiny rubber bands. Some are loops that float anywhere, and some are opened out with their two ends stuck to a sheet of glass. Stack many sheets together. You can describe the stack by what the stuck bands do on the glass, or by how the heavy stack bends the room around it. Two stories, one stack.

Now the real words. In string theory closed strings give gravity and open strings, ending on D-branes, give gauge theory. A stack of N D3-branes is either a gauge theory with N colours (N = 4 super Yang-Mills) or a curved throat, AdS5 × S5.
Maldacena argued these are the same theory. The gauge coupling λ = g²N sets the size of the space in string lengths, and N sets how classical gravity is.
Try it. In the lab, raise N and the coupling until the readout says classical gravity works.
If you remember one thing: the same branes are a gauge theory or a curved space, and each story is easy exactly where the other is hard.
So far holography is a principle. To make it a precise statement you need a theory of quantum gravity in which both sides can be written down. String theory supplies it.
The starting idea of string theory is simple: what we call particles are tiny strings, and different particles are different notes on the same string. There are two kinds. Closed strings are loops.
One of their vibrations has exactly the properties of the graviton, the particle of gravity, which is why string theory is a theory of gravity. Open strings have two ends. (See Figure 5.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.1. Open strings end on D-branes and give gauge fields. Closed strings roam free and give gravity.

items: The ends of open strings must sit somewhere: on surfaces called D-branes, discovered to be real dynamical objects by Joseph Polchinski in 1995. A D3-brane is a brane with three dimensions of space.

If you stack $N$ of them on top of each other, an open string can start on any one of the $N$ branes and end on any one, giving $N\times N$ kinds of string. At low energies these behave exactly like the gluons of a gauge theory with $N$ colours.
Here is the crucial step. That same stack of branes can be described in two completely different ways. (See Figure 5.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.2. Two descriptions of N D3-branes: a gauge theory, or a curved throat.

items: Picture one, valid when the strings interact weakly. The branes are sheets in flat space. The physics on them is a gauge theory called $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang-Mills with gauge group $SU(N)$. This theory happens to be a conformal field theory: it has no length scale at all.
Picture two, valid when the stack is heavy. Branes have mass, and mass curves space. The stack disappears and is replaced by a curved geometry with a deep throat.
Far down the throat the geometry is five-dimensional AdS times a five-dimensional sphere, written $AdS_5\times S^5$, both with the same radius $L$.

In 1997 Juan Maldacena took the low-energy limit of both pictures. In each, the physics splits into two parts that stop talking to each other, and one part is the same in both (free gravity far away). So the other parts must be equal too:

lesson.tex: \mathcal{N}=4 \ \text{super Yang-Mills with } SU(N) \;\;=\;\; \text{string theory on } AdS_5\times S^5

items: A four-dimensional theory without gravity equals a theory of quantum gravity in a higher-dimensional curved space. The four dimensions are the boundary of the $AdS_5$. This is the holographic principle, realised exactly.

The gauge theory has two knobs: the number of colours $N$ and the coupling $g$. The string side has the size of the space $L$ in string lengths $\ell_s$, and Newton's constant $G$ which controls quantum gravity effects. The map between them is the heart of the matter: (See Table 5.1 below.)

rows: strong coupling = space much bigger than a string

items: Read the first relation carefully. When the gauge theory is strongly coupled ($\lambda$ large), where ordinary calculation is hopeless, the curved space is large and smooth and Einstein's gravity works beautifully.
When the gauge theory is weakly coupled and easy, the space is so curved that strings feel it and gravity is useless. (See Figure 5.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.3. Each description is easy exactly where the other is hard.

items: This is why the duality is both powerful and hard to prove. It is powerful because it swaps a hard problem for an easy one. It is hard to prove because you can rarely compute the same thing on both sides.

It has nevertheless passed every test devised in more than twenty-five years, using quantities protected by symmetry, exact methods such as integrability and localization, and computer simulation. (See Table 5.2 below.)

summary: A duality is only useful with a dictionary: a rule for translating each quantity on one side into a quantity on the other.
The master rule equates the two partition functions. From it follow the pairings: a bulk field for every boundary operator, with the field's mass fixing the operator's scaling dimension.
The radial depth z of the bulk is the energy scale of the boundary theory. Moving inward is a renormalization group flow.

Each boundary operator O pairs with a bulk field φ.

Near the boundary φ ≈ φ0 z^(d−Δ) + ⟨O⟩ z^Δ: source and response.
Depth z is inverse energy: the boundary is the UV, the deep bulk is the IR.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Strings, branes and Maldacena's duality:
• Closed strings contain gravity; open strings on D-branes give gauge theory.
• N D3-branes: gauge theory SU(N) on the branes, or a curved throat AdS5 × S5.
• Maldacena: N = 4 super Yang-Mills = string theory on AdS5 × S5.
• L/ℓs = λ^(1/4): strong coupling means a big, gently curved space.
• G ∝ 1/N²: many colours means classical gravity.

ELI5. Imagine two people who speak different languages describing the same film. To check they mean the same thing you need a dictionary. And imagine looking at a painting: with your nose on it you see brush strokes, from across the room you see the picture.
Now the real words. The dictionary says the two theories have equal partition functions when the boundary values of bulk fields are the sources of boundary operators.

Each bulk field matches one operator, and its mass fixes the operator's scaling dimension through Δ(Δ − d) = m²L². The depth z of the bulk is the zoom level of the boundary theory: near the boundary is fine detail and high energy, deep inside is the big picture and low energy.
Try it. In the lab, set the mass to zero and read off dimension 4, then push it down to the lowest allowed value.
If you remember one thing: every bulk field has a boundary partner, and depth is energy scale.
If two theories are the same, there must be a translation between them. The translation manual of AdS/CFT is called the dictionary. (See Figure 6.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 6.1. The holographic dictionary: each bulk object has a boundary partner.

items: The master entry was written down in 1998 by Gubser, Klebanov and Polyakov, and by Witten. In a quantum field theory you learn everything by poking it: add a source $\phi_0(x)$ coupled to an operator $O(x)$ and see how the theory responds.
All the responses are packed into the partition function $Z_{CFT}[\phi_0]$. The rule is

lesson.tex: Z_{CFT}[\phi_0] \;=\; Z_{gravity}\big[\phi \to \phi_0 \text{ at the boundary}\big] \;\approx\; e^{-S_{gravity}[\phi_{classical}]}

items: In words: turning a knob in the boundary theory is the same as fixing the value of a bulk field at the edge of AdS. When gravity is classical (large $N$, large $\lambda$) the right-hand side is easy: solve the classical field equations with that boundary value and evaluate the action.
So every operator has a partner field. What decides which operator? Solve the wave equation for a field of mass $m$ in AdS and look near the boundary $z\to0$. There are always two behaviours:

The slowly falling piece is the source $\phi_0$, the knob you control. The fast falling piece is the response: its coefficient is (up to a constant) the expectation value $\langle O\rangle$ of the dual operator.
And the number $\Delta$ that appears, fixed by the mass, is exactly the operator's scaling dimension. (See Table 6.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 6.1. Mass and dimension for a four-dimensional boundary (d = 4)
head: m²L²
Δ
Example
rows: a relevant operator, such as a mass term
the dilaton, dual to the gauge kinetic term Tr F²

items: Notice that slightly negative $m^2$ is allowed. In flat space a negative mass squared means instability. In AdS the curvature helps, and the field is stable as long as $m^2L^2 \ge -d^2/4$, the Breitenlohner-Freedman bound. Below it, $\Delta$ would be complex and no sensible operator exists.
(See Table 6.2 below.)

lesson.title: Table 6.2. The main dictionary entries
head: Bulk
Boundary

rows: bulk gauge symmetry ↔ boundary global symmetry

items: To compute how operators are correlated, differentiate with respect to the sources. In the bulk this becomes a sum of pictures called Witten diagrams: lines running from boundary points into the bulk, meeting at interaction points that are integrated over all of AdS. (See Figure 6.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 6.2. Witten diagrams for two-, three- and four-point functions.

items: The simplest diagram, a single line between two boundary points, reproduces the power law $1/|x|^{2\Delta}$ of chapter 4. That is a real check: a calculation in curved space gives the answer that conformal symmetry demands.

Finally, the meaning of the extra dimension. Recall that scaling $(t,x,z)$ together is a symmetry. A blob of size $z$ deep in the bulk corresponds to an excitation of size $z$ in the boundary theory. Small $z$ means fine detail and high energy; large $z$ means coarse features and low energy.
(See Figure 6.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 6.3. The radial direction is energy scale. Moving inward blurs out detail.

items: Physicists call the process of zooming out and keeping only coarse features the renormalization group, RG. Holography turns RG into geometry: one step of RG is one step into the bulk.

If the bulk ends at some depth, a wall or a horizon, the boundary theory has a lowest energy scale: a mass gap, or a temperature. This idea is the bridge to tensor networks in chapter 9 and to deep learning in chapter 11.
Memory trick: Mass makes dimension, depth makes energy. The Mass of the field makes the Dimension of the operator; Depth z is one over Energy.

chapters.title: Entanglement builds geometry

maps.title: Entanglement
links: RT formula | corrected by | Bulk entropy
Bulk entropy | leads to | Quantum extremal surface

summary: In 2006 Ryu and Takayanagi found the dictionary entry for entanglement: the entanglement entropy of a boundary region equals the area of the smallest bulk surface that ends on it, divided by 4G.
The formula has the same shape as black hole entropy, but it works for any region. It reproduces the logarithmic law of two-dimensional CFTs and makes hard entropy inequalities obvious.
It also suggests something radical: the connectedness of space is made of entanglement. Remove the entanglement and space comes apart.

glossary.def: S(A) = Area(γ_A)/4G, with γ_A the minimal bulk surface anchored on the edge of A.
The surface of least area with a given boundary; in AdS3, a geodesic.
The requirement that the surface, together with A, encloses a bulk region.
The bulk region between A and its RT surface.
The version of the RT surface for situations that change in time (Hubeny, Rangamani, Takayanagi).
The surface that extremises area/4G plus the bulk entanglement entropy.

keyPoints: RT: S(A) = Area(γ_A)/4G for the minimal surface anchored on A.
In AdS3 the surface is a geodesic of length 2L ln(ℓ/ε), giving S = (c/3) ln(ℓ/ε) with c = 3L/2G.
The minimal surface can jump between competing shapes: a phase transition in entanglement.
Quantum correction: S = Area/4G + S_bulk.
Less entanglement between two boundary parts means a thinner bulk connection (Van Raamsdonk).

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, The dictionary:
• Z_CFT[source φ0] = Z_gravity[field → φ0 at the boundary].
• Each boundary operator O pairs with a bulk field φ.
• Mass fixes dimension: Δ(Δ − d) = m²L².
• Near the boundary φ ≈ φ0 z^(d−Δ) + ⟨O⟩ z^Δ: source and response.
• Depth z is inverse energy: the boundary is the UV, the deep bulk is the IR.

ELI5. Imagine a soap film stretched across a wire loop. It pulls itself into the smallest possible surface. Now imagine that the size of that film tells you how strongly the part of a puzzle inside the loop is linked to the part outside.
Now the real words. The Ryu-Takayanagi formula says the entanglement entropy of a boundary region equals the area of the smallest bulk surface ending on it, divided by 4G.

In AdS3 the surface is a curve, and its length gives exactly the (c/3) ln ℓ law of conformal field theory. Remove the entanglement between two halves of the boundary and the bulk between them pinches off: space is held together by entanglement.
Try it. In the lab, drag the ends of a region and watch the gold curve dip deeper as the region grows.
If you remember one thing: entanglement is measured by area, so geometry is made of entanglement.

The dictionary of the last chapter translates fields and operators. But the boundary theory is a quantum system with a huge amount of entanglement. What does entanglement look like in the bulk? In 2006 Shinsei Ryu and Tadashi Takayanagi proposed a strikingly simple answer. (See Figure 7.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 7.1. The Ryu-Takayanagi formula: entropy of region A is the area of the minimal surface γ_A over 4G.

items: Take a region $A$ of the boundary at one moment of time. Among all bulk surfaces that end on the edge of $A$ (and can be smoothly pushed onto $A$), find the one with the smallest area, $\gamma_A$.
Its area in Planck units, divided by four, is the entanglement entropy of $A$ with the rest of the boundary.

This looks just like the black hole formula $S = A/4G$ from chapter 1, and that is no accident: for a thermal state the minimal surface wraps the horizon, and the formula becomes Bekenstein and Hawking's. Ryu-Takayanagi is the generalisation of black hole entropy to any region.

Let us test it where we know the answer. Take $AdS_3$, whose boundary is one-dimensional, so region $A$ is an interval of length $\ell$ and a 'surface' is just a curve. The minimal curve is a geodesic, the semicircle of chapter 2.
Its length is infinite, because the boundary is infinitely far away, so we stop at a small depth $z=\epsilon$:
The last step uses a result from 1986 by Brown and Henneaux: gravity in $AdS_3$ has the symmetries of a two-dimensional CFT with central charge $c = 3L/2G$.

So the geometric calculation gives exactly the logarithmic law of chapter 4. The mysterious logarithm is the length of a curve in hyperbolic space, and the cutoff $\epsilon$ is where we stop near the boundary. (See Table 7.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 7.1. What the RT formula makes easy
head: Property

items: The minimal surface is found by a competition, and competitions can have sudden changes of winner. Take two separate intervals. Either each gets its own curve, or two curves bridge between them. (See Figure 7.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 7.2. For two regions, the minimal surface jumps from separate curves to bridging curves as the regions grow.

items: When the intervals are small and far apart, separate curves win, and the mutual information $I(A:B)=S(A)+S(B)-S(AB)$ is zero at this order.

Enlarge them and the bridging curves become shorter: the bulk region belonging to $A\cup B$, its entanglement wedge, suddenly becomes connected, and the mutual information turns on. You will find this switch in the lab.
The formula has since been extended. Hubeny, Rangamani and Takayanagi (2007) gave the version for geometries that change in time, using extremal instead of minimal surfaces.
Faulkner, Lewkowycz and Maldacena (2013) added the first quantum correction: the entanglement of the bulk fields themselves across the surface.

Engelhardt and Wall (2014) then proposed that the right surface is the one that extremises this whole sum, the quantum extremal surface. Keep this in mind: it is the tool that resolves the black hole information puzzle in chapter 12. (See Table 7.2 below.)

items: Now turn the formula around. If entanglement is measured by area, then geometry is made of entanglement. Mark Van Raamsdonk made this vivid in 2010. Divide the boundary into two halves and imagine reducing the entanglement between them.

By RT the surface separating the two halves of the bulk must shrink. At the same time the mutual information between distant points drops, which means they get further apart. The space stretches and pinches. (See Figure 7.3 below.)

summary: Heat the boundary theory and a black hole forms in the bulk. Its temperature is the temperature of the boundary theory, and its horizon area is the thermal entropy.
Below a critical temperature the black hole is not the preferred geometry: the Hawking-Page transition, which the boundary theory sees as the change from confined to deconfined matter.
Two copies of the boundary theory in a special entangled state describe a single black hole with two outsides joined by a wormhole. Entanglement is the bridge.

glossary.def: The temperature at which a black hole radiates.
The black hole of three-dimensional AdS gravity.
A system in equilibrium at a temperature T; a mixed state.
The switch between thermal AdS and a black hole as the dominant geometry.
An entangled state of two copies of a system in which each copy alone is thermal.
The wormhole connecting the two sides of an eternal black hole.
The slogan that wormholes (ER) and entanglement (EPR) are the same thing.

keyPoints: Thermal state of the CFT ↔ black hole in AdS; horizon area/4G = thermal entropy.
BTZ: T = r_h/(2πL²), S = 2πr_h/4G, matching the CFT's Cardy formula.
Hawking-Page: below T = 1/(2πL) thermal AdS wins; above it the black hole wins.
With a horizon, S(A) ≠ S(rest); the difference for large A is the black hole entropy.
Thermofield double = eternal two-sided black hole; the entanglement is the wormhole.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Entanglement builds geometry:
• RT: S(A) = Area(γ_A)/4G for the minimal surface anchored on A.
• In AdS3 the surface is a geodesic of length 2L ln(ℓ/ε), giving S = (c/3) ln(ℓ/ε) with c = 3L/2G.
• The minimal surface can jump between competing shapes: a phase transition in entanglement.
• Quantum correction: S = Area/4G + S_bulk.
• Less entanglement between two boundary parts means a thinner bulk connection (Van Raamsdonk).

ELI5. Imagine heating a pan of soup. From outside, all you know is how hot it is; the details are hidden. In the bulk world, heating the edge makes a black hole appear in the middle. And imagine two walkie-talkies that are secretly linked: in the bulk world, that secret link is a tunnel.

Now the real words. A black hole in the bulk is a thermal state of the boundary theory; the horizon area over 4G is the thermal entropy. Below the Hawking-Page temperature the bulk is just warm empty AdS, and above it a black hole wins, which the boundary sees as deconfinement.
Two copies of the boundary theory entangled in the thermofield double state are the two outsides of one black hole joined by a wormhole: ER = EPR.
Try it. In the lab, cool the system below 0.159 and watch the black hole stop being the winner.
If you remember one thing: hot means a horizon, and entanglement between two systems is a bridge between two spaces.

What is a black hole in the boundary theory? There is no gravity there, so it cannot be a black hole. The dictionary answer is beautifully simple: a black hole in the bulk is the boundary theory at a temperature. Hot soup.

The reasoning: a black hole has a temperature (Hawking) and an entropy (Bekenstein). A quantum system with a temperature and an entropy is a thermal state. The energy of the black hole is the energy of the hot matter, and the area of the horizon divided by $4G$ is its entropy.
The cleanest example is the black hole of three-dimensional AdS gravity, found by Bañados, Teitelboim and Zanelli (BTZ) in 1992:
The horizon is at $r = r_h$, where the coefficient of $dt^2$ vanishes: time stands still there for an outside observer. Its temperature and entropy are

The last form uses $c = 3L/2G$. It says the entropy is $\pi c/3$ times the length of the boundary circle, $2\pi L$, times the temperature. That is exactly Cardy's formula for the entropy of any two-dimensional CFT at high temperature. Gravity counts the CFT's states correctly. (See Table 8.1 below.)

items: Is a black hole always the right bulk description of a hot state? No. Hawking and Page showed in 1983 that there are two competing geometries with the same temperature at the boundary: empty AdS filled with a gas of hot particles (thermal AdS), and a black hole.
The one with the lower free energy $F$ wins. (See Figure 8.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 8.1. The Hawking-Page transition: thermal AdS at low temperature, a black hole at high temperature.

items: In three dimensions the switch happens at $T = 1/(2\pi L)$. Witten pointed out in 1998 what this means for the gauge theory: at low temperature its entropy is small (the colour charges are confined into a few bound states), while at high temperature it jumps to order $N^2$ (the $N^2$ gluons are set free). The formation of a black hole is deconfinement.

A horizon changes entanglement. For a small region the RT curve stays outside the horizon and barely notices it. For a large region it becomes cheaper to take the short curve around the complement and add the whole horizon. (See Figure 8.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 8.2. RT curves in a black hole geometry. Large regions pay for the horizon.

items: For $\ell$ much smaller than $\beta$ this is the old logarithm. For $\ell$ much larger it grows in proportion to $\ell$: a volume law, as a thermal state should have. And because the state is mixed, $S(A)$ no longer equals $S(\bar A)$. For large $A$ the difference is exactly the black hole entropy.

Where did the purity go? A thermal state is mixed, but any mixed state can be seen as half of a pure entangled state of a bigger system. Take two copies of the CFT, call them left and right, in the thermofield double state:

Each copy alone is exactly thermal. In 2001 Maldacena proposed that the bulk dual is the eternal black hole: one geometry with two outside regions, each with its own boundary, joined through the interior by an Einstein-Rosen bridge, a wormhole. (See Figure 8.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 8.3. The thermofield double state is dual to a two-sided black hole. The entanglement is the bridge.

items: The two CFTs do not interact at all. They are only entangled. Yet in the bulk their spaces are joined. The RT surface between left and right is the horizon, and its area is the entanglement entropy between the two copies.

Maldacena and Susskind compressed this in 2013 into the slogan ER = EPR: Einstein-Rosen bridges and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen entanglement are two descriptions of one thing. The bridge cannot be used to send signals, just as entanglement cannot. (See Table 8.2 below.)

summary: A tensor network builds a big quantum state out of small pieces joined by bonds. The pattern of bonds controls the pattern of entanglement.

Coarse-graining a quantum system step by step produces a layered network with an extra direction: scale. For a critical system the network has the shape of hyperbolic space, and the entropy of a region is bounded by the cheapest cut through the bonds, a discrete Ryu-Takayanagi formula.

Special networks built from 'perfect' or random tensors make this exact, and they are also error-correcting codes. They are toy models: simple enough to count, rich enough to show how holography works.

glossary.def: A block of numbers with several indices, drawn as a shape with legs.
A leg shared by two tensors; it carries entanglement.
The number of values a bond index can take; a bond carries at most log χ of entanglement.
Replacing groups of sites by fewer effective sites, keeping long-distance physics.
Multiscale entanglement renormalization ansatz: a layered network for critical states.
The smallest set of bonds whose removal separates a region from the rest.
A tensor that is maximally entangled across every equal split of its legs.
A network whose tensors are chosen at random; its entropies obey a minimal-cut rule.

keyPoints: A tensor network's bonds limit entanglement: S(A) ≤ (bonds cut) × log χ.
Coarse-graining adds a direction: N sites need about log N layers.
MERA reproduces S ∝ log ℓ; its shape resembles a slice of AdS (Swingle 2009).
Random and perfect-tensor networks saturate the bound: entropy = minimal cut, a discrete RT formula.
They are toy models: discrete, without full dynamics, but exactly solvable.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Black holes, temperature and wormholes:
• Thermal state of the CFT ↔ black hole in AdS; horizon area/4G = thermal entropy.
• BTZ: T = r_h/(2πL²), S = 2πr_h/4G, matching the CFT's Cardy formula.
• Hawking-Page: below T = 1/(2πL) thermal AdS wins; above it the black hole wins.
• With a horizon, S(A) ≠ S(rest); the difference for large A is the black hole entropy.
• Thermofield double = eternal two-sided black hole; the entanglement is the wormhole.

ELI5. Imagine describing a huge crowd. First you group people into families, then families into streets, then streets into towns. Each step gives a smaller, blurrier picture. Stack the pictures up and you get a pyramid. To separate one neighbourhood from the rest, the cheapest place to cut the pyramid is higher up, where there are fewer links.
Now the real words. A tensor network builds a quantum state from small tensors joined by bonds. The entropy of a region is limited by the bonds you must cut to separate it.

Coarse-graining adds a direction, scale, and for a critical state the network has the shape of hyperbolic space, with the cheapest cut playing the role of the Ryu-Takayanagi surface. With perfect or random tensors the limit becomes exact.
Try it. In the lab, select 2, 4, 8 and 16 sites and see the cut cost go up by about the same amount each time.
If you remember one thing: count the bonds on the cheapest cut: that is the entropy, and that is the minimal surface.

A quantum state of $n$ qubits needs $2^n$ numbers. For 300 qubits that is more numbers than atoms in the visible universe. Tensor networks are a way to write interesting states with far fewer numbers, by building them out of small blocks.

A tensor is just a block of numbers with several indices. Draw it as a dot or box with one leg per index. Joining two legs means summing over that index. A leg joined between two tensors is called a bond; a leg left dangling is a physical qubit.
The key fact: a bond that can take $\chi$ values can carry at most $\log\chi$ of entanglement. So to see how entangled a region can be, count the bonds you must cut to separate it:

Now the idea that creates an extra dimension. To understand a big system, physicists coarse-grain: replace each pair of neighbouring sites by one effective site that keeps only what matters at larger distances, and repeat. Each round halves the number of sites. (See Figure 9.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.1. Repeated coarse-graining stacks into a tree. Its height is a new direction: scale.

items: Read the tree upside down and it is a recipe for building the state: start from a few coarse sites and add detail layer by layer. The layers are a new direction, and it measures scale, exactly like the depth $z$ in AdS. A system of $N$ sites needs about $\log_2 N$ layers.

A plain tree loses too much entanglement between neighbouring blocks. Guifré Vidal's MERA (2007) fixes this by adding extra tensors that remove short-range entanglement before each coarse-graining step. The result describes critical states very well. Now cut out a block of $\ell$ sites.
(See Figure 9.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.2. In a layered network, the cheapest cut around a block of sites climbs to the sparse upper layers.

items: The cheapest cut does not hug the block. It rises through the layers, where there are fewer bonds, and comes down the other side, cutting a couple of bonds per layer over about $\log\ell$ layers. So $S \propto \log\ell$: the logarithmic law of a critical system, from pure counting.

In 2009 Brian Swingle pointed out that this is the Ryu-Takayanagi formula in disguise. The network is a discrete picture of a slice of AdS; the cheapest cut is the minimal surface; cutting more bonds is having more area.
Hyperbolic space is simply the shape a network must have to hold the entanglement of a scale-invariant state. (See Table 9.1 below.)

head: State

rows: a thin shell: the bulk ends

items: A general network only gives an upper bound on entropy. Two special constructions turn the bound into an equality, a true discrete RT formula.

The first uses perfect tensors: tensors so evenly entangled that any half of their legs is maximally entangled with the other half. In 2015 Pastawski, Yoshida, Harlow and Preskill tiled the hyperbolic plane with six-leg perfect tensors, one per pentagon.
Five legs join the neighbours; the sixth points out of the page and is a bulk qubit. The legs left at the rim are the boundary. (See Figure 9.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.3. The HaPPY code: perfect tensors on a pentagon tiling of the hyperbolic plane.

items: This is called the HaPPY code after its authors. In it, the entropy of a connected boundary region is exactly the number of bonds on the minimal cut. And it is more than a state: it is a map from bulk qubits to boundary qubits, an error-correcting code. That is the subject of the next chapter.

The second construction uses random tensors (Hayden, Nezami, Qi, Thomas, Walter and Yang, 2016). If every tensor is chosen at random and the bond dimension is large, the entropy of any boundary region is, to excellent accuracy, the minimal cut times $\log\chi$.

The calculation maps the network onto a simple magnet, an Ising model whose couplings are set by the bond dimensions. Hold on to that fact: an Ising model with adjustable couplings is a kind of neural network, and that is the bridge of chapter 11. (See Table 9.2 below.)

items: A caution. These are toy models. They capture how entanglement and geometry fit together on one slice of time, but they do not contain gravity's dynamics, and they are discrete where AdS is smooth. Their value is that you can count everything, as you will in the lab.

summary: A quantum error-correcting code hides a little protected information inside a lot of noisy hardware, by spreading it out in entanglement. No small piece of the hardware knows the secret, yet it survives the loss of some pieces.

The way the bulk sits inside the boundary theory is exactly like that. The bulk is the protected logical information; the boundary degrees of freedom are the physical hardware; losing a boundary region is an erasure.

This view explains how a bulk point can be rebuilt from many different boundary regions without contradiction, which region can rebuild what (the entanglement wedge), and where the Ryu-Takayanagi area term comes from.

glossary.def: A way to store quantum information in a larger system so that it survives some errors.
Logical: the protected information. Physical: the actual hardware carrying it.
The small set of physical states used to represent logical states.
An error where you lose known qubits completely.
The mathematical test for whether a set of errors can be corrected.
Writing a bulk operator as a boundary operator.
The statement that a boundary region A describes a definite bulk region.
The bulk region between A and its RT surface: what A can reconstruct.
Quantum information cannot be copied.

keyPoints: Codes hide logical information in entanglement among many physical qubits.
Three-qutrit code: no single qutrit knows the secret; any two recover it.
The low-energy bulk is a code subspace of the CFT: H_code ⊂ H_CFT.
A bulk operator in the entanglement wedge of A can be reconstructed on A alone.
Different reconstructions agree only on the code subspace, so nothing is cloned; the RT area term is part of the code's structure.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Tensor networks: holograms you can count:
• A tensor network's bonds limit entanglement: S(A) ≤ (bonds cut) × log χ.
• Coarse-graining adds a direction: N sites need about log N layers.
• MERA reproduces S ∝ log ℓ; its shape resembles a slice of AdS (Swingle 2009).
• Random and perfect-tensor networks saturate the bound: entropy = minimal cut, a discrete RT formula.
• They are toy models: discrete, without full dynamics, but exactly solvable.

ELI5. Imagine three friends who each hold a piece of a treasure map. No single piece shows anything. Any two friends can put theirs together and find the treasure. Lose one friend and the secret is still safe.

Now the real words. That is the three-qutrit code, a quantum error-correcting code. Holography works the same way: the bulk is the protected, logical information, and the boundary is the physical hardware.

A boundary region can rebuild exactly the bulk points in its entanglement wedge. The same bulk point can be rebuilt from different regions, but the different versions agree only on the code subspace of smooth-bulk states, so nothing is copied. Deeper points survive bigger losses.
Try it. In the lab, erase each qutrit in turn and recover the message from the other two.
If you remember one thing: the bulk is a secret shared across the boundary, and depth is protection.
Quantum information is fragile, and it cannot be copied: that is the no-cloning theorem. So you cannot protect it the classical way, by keeping three copies and taking a vote.
Quantum error correction protects it differently: it spreads the information across many qubits in a pattern of entanglement so that no small group of qubits contains it.
The simplest example that matters for us uses qutrits, three-level systems with states $|0\rangle,|1\rangle,|2\rangle$. One logical qutrit is stored in three physical ones. (See Figure 10.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 10.1. The three-qutrit code. One qutrit alone knows nothing; any two can recover the logical state.

items: Look at any one physical qutrit in any of these states: it is 0, 1 or 2 with equal probability, whatever the logical state is. It has learned nothing. But any two qutrits together determine the logical state completely, so the code survives the loss, the erasure, of any one qutrit.

There is a further consequence: the same logical operation can be carried out by acting on qutrits 1 and 2 only, or on 2 and 3 only, or on 3 and 1 only. Three different physical operators, one logical effect.
The general test for whether a code can correct a set of errors $E_i$ is the Knill-Laflamme condition. With $P$ the projector onto the code subspace:

In words: the errors may scramble the hardware, but they must not be able to tell different logical states apart, and must not confuse one logical state with another. The numbers $\lambda_{ij}$ do not depend on the logical state.
Now the puzzle that brought error correction into gravity. A bulk field at a point $x$ should be expressible as some operator of the boundary theory; this is called bulk reconstruction.

Techniques developed in the 2000s showed that a bulk operator can be rebuilt using only the boundary region whose bulk 'wedge' contains it. But one bulk point lies in the wedges of many different regions. (See Figure 10.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 10.2. The centre point x can be reconstructed from any two of the three boundary arcs, but from no single arc.

items: Divide the boundary into three arcs $A$, $B$, $C$. A field at the centre can be reconstructed on $A\cup B$, or on $B\cup C$, or on $C\cup A$.

If these were literally the same operator, it would have to commute with everything in $C$, and in $A$, and in $B$, which means with every local operator of the boundary theory. Then it would be trivial. That cannot be right.

In 2014 Almheiri, Dong and Harlow saw the resolution: this is exactly the three-qutrit code. The three reconstructions are different boundary operators that act in the same way only on a special set of states, the code subspace. The bulk is logical information; the boundary theory is the hardware.
(See Figure 10.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 10.3. The states that look like a smooth bulk form a small code subspace of the boundary theory.

items: Here $\phi(x)$ is the bulk (logical) operator and $\Phi_A$ is a boundary (physical) operator supported only on region $A$ that represents it. The code subspace consists of the states that look like a given smooth spacetime with a few particles on it.
Outside the code subspace, in states with a big black hole for instance, $\Phi_A$ and $\Phi_B$ may act quite differently. (See Table 10.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 10.1. The error-correction dictionary
head: Quantum error correction
Holography
rows: states describing a smooth bulk with few excitations
losing access to a boundary region
the bulk point lies in the entanglement wedge of what remains
deeper bulk points survive larger erasures

items: Which region can reconstruct which bulk points? The answer, established by Dong, Harlow and Wall in 2016 building on a result of Jafferis, Lewkowycz, Maldacena and Suh, is the entanglement wedge: the bulk region between $A$ and its Ryu-Takayanagi surface.
There is a neat test, the commutant criterion. A logical operator $O$ can be reconstructed on $A$ exactly when, on the code subspace, it commutes with everything on the complement $\bar A$:

lesson.tex: \text{for every } X_{\bar A} \text{ on the complement}

items: Intuitively: if nothing done in $\bar A$ can disturb $O$, then $O$ did not live there, so it can be reached from $A$. This is also why nothing is cloned.
A piece of bulk information can be read from $A$ or from another region $B$, but those two readings are not independent copies: acting with one changes what the other finds.

The result underneath is a statement about relative entropy, which measures how distinguishable two states are. The JLMS relation says that two states are exactly as distinguishable on boundary region $A$ as they are in the bulk entanglement wedge of $A$.
It follows from a refinement of RT in which the area appears as an operator:

$K$ is the modular Hamiltonian, the logarithm of the density matrix. Harlow showed in 2016 that this structure is not an accident of gravity: any code with complementary recovery (whatever $A$ cannot reconstruct, $\bar A$ can) automatically has an entropy formula of the form 'area term plus bulk entropy'.

The area term belongs to the part of the code shared by both sides, technically the centre of the operator algebra. The Ryu-Takayanagi formula is the signature of an error-correcting code. (See Table 10.2 below.)

lesson.title: Table 10.2. Common confusions
head: Confusion
Clarification
rows: 'The bulk operator is stored in one place on the boundary.'
No: it has many representatives on different regions, all equal on the code subspace.
No: they are the same logical operator; no-cloning is respected.
Only for the code subspace; with big black holes reconstruction becomes state-dependent.
They are toy models that show the mechanism, not the full theory.
In real holography it is approximate, with errors controlled by 1/N and by how small G is.

items: Why would nature build a code? Because gravity needs locality in the bulk to emerge from a boundary theory that has no idea the bulk exists. A point deep in the bulk is the best-protected information there is: you must lose more than half the boundary before it is gone.
Points near the boundary are barely protected. Depth is protection.

summary: A deep neural network processes data layer by layer, keeping what matters and discarding detail. So does the renormalization group, and so does the radial direction of AdS. The resemblance can be made into working algorithms.

In entanglement feature learning, a network is trained on the entanglement entropies of a quantum state. The trained network's connectivity is an emergent geometry, and for a critical state it comes out hyperbolic.

In the 'AdS/CFT as a deep network' approach, the radial direction is discretised into layers and the bulk metric is the set of weights, learned from boundary data. These are bridges under construction: suggestive and useful, not finished theorems.

glossary.def: A function built from layers of simple units with adjustable weights.
The numbers a network learns; here, bond strengths or the bulk metric.
A number measuring how wrong the network's output is.
Improving the weights step by step in the direction that lowers the loss.
A network of binary units with an energy function; learning shapes its probability distribution.
Visible units face the data; hidden units capture structure.

A geometry that is not put in by hand but read off from the learned connections.

keyPoints: Depth in a network, steps of RG and radial depth in AdS all organise information by scale.
Random tensor network entropies = free energy of an Ising model = a Boltzmann machine.
EFL: fit the couplings to entanglement data; the learned graph is the bulk geometry.
Critical data in, hyperbolic geometry out; gapped data gives a shallow network.
AdS/DL: radial slices = layers, metric = weights, boundary data = training set.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Holography is a quantum error-correcting code:
• Codes hide logical information in entanglement among many physical qubits.
• Three-qutrit code: no single qutrit knows the secret; any two recover it.
• The low-energy bulk is a code subspace of the CFT: H_code ⊂ H_CFT.
• A bulk operator in the entanglement wedge of A can be reconstructed on A alone.
• Different reconstructions agree only on the code subspace, so nothing is cloned; the RT area term is part of the code's structure.

ELI5. Imagine a guessing machine made of dials. You show it examples, it checks how wrong it is, and it turns every dial a tiny bit to be less wrong. After many rounds the dials hold what it has learned. Now imagine the dials are the strengths of the links in our pyramid of blurry pictures.

Now the real words. A neural network learns by gradient descent on a loss. A random tensor network's entropies are the free energies of an Ising model, which is a Boltzmann machine, so the network can be trained on a quantum state's entanglement entropies.

The trained couplings are a geometry nobody put in, and for a critical state it is hyperbolic. In another approach the radial direction of AdS is the layers of a network and the metric is the weights.
Try it. In the lab, press Train on critical data and watch every layer stay switched on; then try gapped data and watch the deep layers fade.
If you remember one thing: the geometry can be learned from entanglement, with bond strengths as the weights.

Three ladders in this course look alike. A deep network turns raw pixels into edges, shapes and finally 'cat'. The renormalization group turns microscopic spins into blocks and finally a description of the long-distance physics.
The bulk of AdS runs from the boundary, where all the fine detail lives, into the deep interior. (See Figure 11.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 11.1. Deep networks, renormalization and the AdS radial direction: three ladders organised by scale.

items: In each case every step keeps what is relevant at the next scale and forgets the rest. Mehta and Schwab (2014) made the first link precise in a simple setting: stacking a certain kind of network, the restricted Boltzmann machine, performs a form of RG coarse-graining on spin systems.
The second link, RG as the radial direction, was chapter 6. Can we close the triangle and connect learning directly to holographic geometry?

First, the machinery of learning, in four words: weights, loss, gradient, repeat. A network has adjustable numbers, the weights $w$. A loss function $\mathcal L(w)$ measures how far its output is from the data. Gradient descent changes every weight a little in the direction that lowers the loss:
with a small step size $\eta$. Repeat many times. That is all 'training' means. In the labs you will press a Train button that does exactly this.

Bridge one: entanglement feature learning. This is the subject of Yi-Zhuang You's Perimeter Institute talk 'Tensor Network Holography and Deep Learning' (2017), based on work with Zhao Yang and Xiao-Liang Qi.

Recall from chapter 9 that in a random tensor network the entropy of a boundary region is a minimal cut, and that the calculation maps onto an Ising model, a magnet whose spins sit on the tensors and whose couplings are set by the bond dimensions.
Precisely: the entanglement entropy of region $A$ is the free energy cost of forcing the boundary spins in $A$ to point down while the rest point up.

lesson.tex: S(A) \;\approx\; F\big[\text{spins down on } A\big] - F\big[\text{all spins up}\big]

items: An Ising model with adjustable couplings, with some spins exposed to data and some hidden, is a Boltzmann machine: one of the classic neural networks. The boundary spins are the visible units.
The bulk spins are the hidden units. The couplings $J_{ij}$ are the weights. So a random tensor network is a neural network, and its 'data' are entanglement entropies. (See Figure 11.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 11.2. Entanglement feature learning: train a network on entanglement entropies and read off the geometry.

items: The algorithm: take a quantum state, here the ground state of free fermions on a line. Compute the entanglement entropy of many regions; these are the 'entanglement features'. Start with a deep network whose couplings are unknown.

Train the couplings by gradient descent until the model's entropies match the data. Then look at the trained network: strong couplings mean 'close', weak couplings mean 'far'. That pattern of connections is a geometry nobody put in.
The result reported in the talk: as the fermion system is tuned towards its critical point, where it becomes a two-dimensional CFT, the learned network becomes hyperbolic, like a slice of $AdS_3$.

Away from criticality the deep layers decouple and the bulk is cut off at a finite depth, as you would expect for a system with a correlation length. Holographic geometry emerges from learning the entanglement. (See Table 11.1 below.)

lesson.title: Table 11.1. Entanglement feature learning, term by term
head: Machine learning
Tensor network
Holography
rows: mismatch of model and measured entropies

items: Bridge two: AdS/CFT as a deep neural network. In 2018 Hashimoto, Sugishita, Tanaka and Tomiya turned the dictionary of chapter 6 into a network directly. A bulk field obeys a wave equation in the radial direction. Cut the radial coordinate into slices.

The field and its radial derivative at one slice are computed from those at the previous slice: that is one layer of a network. The metric function appearing in the equation plays the role of the weights. (See Figure 11.3 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 11.3. The bulk equation of motion, discretised along the radial direction, is a deep network whose weights are the metric.

items: Here $\eta$ is the radial coordinate, $\pi$ is the radial derivative of the field, $V$ is its potential, and $h(\eta)$ is built from the metric: it is the unknown.

The input layer is boundary data (a source and its response, for example an applied magnetic field and the measured magnetisation). The output layer checks the condition a field must satisfy at the black hole horizon.
Training on experimental or simulated response data then learns $h(\eta)$: the network discovers the bulk metric that explains the boundary data.

The authors first applied it to magnetisation data from a real strongly correlated material, and in follow-up work to lattice QCD data, where the learned metric showed the features of a confining geometry. (See Table 11.2 below.)

lesson.title: Table 11.2. Two bridges compared
head: Entanglement feature learning

rows: Boltzmann machine on a layered graph
feed-forward network along the radial direction

items: How far does the analogy go? Be careful here. It is established that RG, tensor networks and certain neural networks share mathematical structure, and that these algorithms work on simple examples.
It is not established that a trained network is a full theory of gravity, or that deep learning in general 'is' holography.

The honest status: a productive dictionary between fields. Physics gains algorithms for finding geometries and for representing quantum states. Machine learning gains ideas about why depth helps and what layers represent.

In the lab you will run a toy version of entanglement feature learning: a layered network whose bond weights are trained by gradient descent to reproduce entropies. Feed it critical data and it grows deep; feed it gapped data and it stays shallow.
Memory trick: Weights are bonds, depth is depth. Learning bridge: Weights are bond strengths, hidden units are bulk points, network Depth is bulk Depth.

chapters.title: Black hole information: the Page curve and islands

maps.title: Information
links: Page curve | turns at | Page time

Island formula | after Page time | Island
